findings.title: Retention purges IN-FLIGHT DSARs because the clock falls back to created_at for open requests
findings.scenario: An operator sets RETENTION_RULES="dsar=365". The docstring promises a DSAR's retention clock starts when it COMPLETED. But an open (never completed) DSAR has completed_at=0.0 (falsy) and no 'resolved_at'/'at' fields, so _clock_field falls through to created_at. A DSAR that has been stuck open for >365 days (e.g. a target that never acked, still on its statutory clock and flagged 'overdue') is therefore deleted by the nightly retention CronJob — destroying the record of an unfulfilled data-subject request, the single worst thing to lose to a regulator.
findings.recommendation: In _clock_field, refuse to age out a row whose collection is 'dsar' unless it is in a terminal state (completed_at/refused set). More generally, do not fall back to created_at for records whose retention clock is defined only in a terminal state; skip (KEEP) rows with no terminal timestamp.
findings.fix: _clock_field(row, collection) never ages out a non-terminal DSAR: an open (no completed_at/refused, non-terminal status) dsar returns None (retain) instead of falling back to created_at, so a request stuck open past the retention window is no longer deleted mid-flight. Regression tests added.

findings.title: Erasure leaves the subject's RAW identifier in the DSAR store and other compliance-owned collections
findings.scenario: ComplianceErasure.erase only touches the 'consent' and 'consent_proof' collections. compliance-service is itself a registered data target (service=compliance-service, category=consent), but its own DSAR rows persist the RAW subject id plus the request payload (Dsar.subject / Dsar.payload), and are never scrubbed or pseudonymised on erasure. After a subject is 'erased' and the DSAR is marked completed, the person's raw identifier and any payload PII remain in the dsar collection (and in every sealed backup of it) indefinitely, contradicting the completeness promise the service exists to enforce.
findings.evidence:
class ComplianceErasure:
    service = "compliance-service"
    category = "consent"
    ...
    rows, cursor = await self._store.find(_CONSENT, {"tenant": tenant, "subject": subject}, ...)
findings.recommendation: Extend erase() to pseudonymise/scrub the subject in the service's own dsar rows (and any other own collection carrying raw subject/payload), or register a distinct category per collection so completion honestly reflects what was left behind.
findings.fix: ComplianceErasure.erase now scrubs the service's OWN dsar rows for the subject (subject->pseudonym, payload->{}) in addition to consent/proof; already_absent accounts for them. The DSAR record survives as evidence, without the raw id/payload. Regression test added.

findings.title: Write-ahead audit records "subject.erased" BEFORE the erase runs, so a hold-blocked erase is logged as a real erasure
findings.scenario: erase_subject records the critical 'subject.erased' audit event write-ahead, then calls eraser.erase(). erase() may return {"blocked_by_legal_hold": True, "erased": []} (an active hold, or an incomplete hold read → fail closed). Nothing was erased, yet the audit chain now contains a 'subject.erased' entry for that subject. The audit trail — the one artefact a regulator reads to confirm what happened — asserts an erasure that legal hold actually prevented.
findings.evidence:
await request.app.state.auditor.record(
        "subject.erased", actor="", tenant=body.tenant, resource=f"subject:{subject_ref(get_settings().PII_SALT, body.tenant, body.subject)}", ...)
    c = request.app.state.container
    eraser = ComplianceErasure(store=c.datastore, pii_salt=s.PII_SALT)
    return await eraser.erase(body.tenant, body.subject)
findings.recommendation: Record the erasure outcome AFTER erase() returns, reflecting blocked_by_legal_hold/hold_check_incomplete (e.g. 'subject.erase_refused'), or gate the write-ahead so a hold-blocked call does not emit 'subject.erased'.
findings.fix: erase_subject records the ACTUAL outcome after erase() returns — subject.erased on success, or a new critical subject.erase_refused when blocked_by_legal_hold/hold_check_incomplete — instead of a write-ahead subject.erased that falsely certified a deletion a hold prevented. erase is idempotent so after-the-fact recording is safe.

findings.title: Guardian/delegated PII (consented_by) is NOT pseudonymised on erasure of the consent proof
findings.scenario: The consent proof is retained but only its 'subject' field is overwritten with the pseudonym. A guardian/legal-representative consent proof also carries consented_by (e.g. the parent's email) and relation as RAW identifiers. Erasing the child leaves the parent's raw identifier sitting in the surviving proof; and erasing the PARENT as a subject never matches proofs where they appear only as consented_by, so their raw id survives regardless. Personal data of a third party remains after an erasure that reported success.
findings.evidence:
for p in page:
                p["subject"] = ref
                await self._store.put(_PROOF, p["id"], p)
                proofs += 1
findings.recommendation: When pseudonymising a surviving proof, also pseudonymise consented_by (and any actor holding a raw identifier) via subject_ref; and add a data-map/erase path that scrubs consented_by occurrences when the represented party is themselves the erasure subject.
findings.fix: a surviving guardian/delegated consent proof now has consented_by pseudonymised (its own subject_ref) on erasure, not just subject — erasing the child no longer leaves the parent's raw identifier in the proof. Regression test added.

findings.title: Operator-created DSAR returns the verification token to the operator, defeating 'identity before PII'
findings.scenario: create_dsar (operator, _ADMIN) returns d.verification_token in the HTTP response. The token exists precisely to prove the SUBJECT controls their channel before any access/export data is released. Handed back to the API caller, an operator with compliance.manage can create an access/export DSAR for ANY subject in the tenant, self-verify with the token they just received, then process() and receive the exported PII fan-out — the verification control provides zero protection on the operator path (the docstring in dsar_service.py calls this the 'best data-exfiltration tool an attacker ever had').
findings.evidence:
if created:
        out["verification_token"] = d.verification_token   # returned ONCE, to send to the subject
findings.recommendation: Do not return the token in the operator-tier response; deliver it only out-of-band to the subject's own channel (the /internal/.../verification-code seam already exists for product-owned delivery). Reserve token return for the /me/dsar self-service path.

findings.title: Write-ahead audit entries are emitted for actions that then 404 / are refused, polluting the trail
findings.scenario: release_hold records 'legal_hold.released' before calling release_hold(), which returns None (→404) when the hold does not exist or belongs to another tenant. The audit chain then contains a 'legal_hold.released' entry for a release that never happened. The same pattern applies to process_dsar (dsar.processed then NOT_FOUND 404), notify_breach, and delete_target — a caller can spray IDs and manufacture audit entries for non-existent resources.
findings.evidence:
await request.app.state.auditor.record(
        "legal_hold.released", actor=principal.subject, tenant=principal.tenant, resource=f"hold:{hold_id}", ...)
    h = await build_compliance(request).release_hold(hold_id, tenant=_tenant(principal))
    if h is None:
        raise HTTPException(404, "NOT_FOUND")
findings.recommendation: For these routes, verify existence/ownership first (or record on the success path), reserving true write-ahead only where the mutation cannot be pre-validated. A refused/absent action must not be logged as though it occurred.

findings.title: ConsentSweeper write-back of a legacy-keyed row creates a duplicate and re-announces every night
findings.scenario: _announce and the derived-lapse write-back store the row under the normalised canonical key (_key) but never DELETE the legacy raw-purpose key it was read from. A consent granted under a pre-normalisation key (purpose with uppercase/whitespace) therefore gets a NEW canonical duplicate carrying the announced flag, while the original legacy row survives unflagged. scan_all returns the legacy row again next run → the guardian is re-emailed 'consent lapsing' every night (the exact outcome the docstring calls 'worse than late'), and the tenant now has two consent rows for one consent.
findings.recommendation: Mirror ConsentStore.put: after writing under the canonical key, delete the legacy key when it differs; or run migrate_purpose_keys before enabling the sweeper. Assert no duplicate (tenant,subject,purpose) rows remain.

findings.title: internal_dsar filters by subject in Python AFTER a capped list(), silently missing a subject's older DSARs
findings.scenario: internal_dsar calls build_dsar().list(tenant) — which reads at most COMPLIANCE_LIST_LIMIT (100) newest DSARs — then filters r['subject']==subject in Python. A subject whose DSARs are not among the tenant's 100 most-recent requests returns {"dsars": [], "count": 0}: the case-timeline tool reports the subject has filed nothing, when they may have several older requests. The subject filter is not pushed down and the fetch is unbounded-by-intent but capped-in-fact.
findings.recommendation: Add a DsarStore.for_subject(tenant, subject) that pushes {tenant, subject} into find() (paginated), and have this route use it instead of filtering a truncated tenant-wide list.

findings.title: Retention scan_all reads an arbitrary insertion-order slice, so rows past the cap are never purged
findings.scenario: _purge calls scan_all(collection, limit=self._max). MemoryDataStore.scan_all (and the port contract) returns the FIRST max rows in storage order, not oldest-first. When a collection holds more than RETENTION_MAX_PER_RUN rows, the same head slice is examined every run and rows beyond the cap are never visited — an expired 2019 row that sorts after the cap is never purged, so the RoPA still claims '365 days' while the row persists (the precise failure this module exists to prevent). The cap silently bounds correctness, not just work.
findings.evidence: rows = await self._store.scan_all(collection, limit=self._max)
findings.recommendation: Page through the collection by the retention clock field (oldest-first) to completion across runs using a cursor, or make scan_all order-defined and rotate the starting offset; treat reaching the cap as 'more work remains', not 'done'.

findings.title: Retention deletions of legal records are not recorded to the audit sink (only a telemetry gauge)
findings.scenario: RetentionEnforcer deletes rows and only emits a telemetry 'retention.run' summary; the audit sink gets one generic write-ahead 'retention.purged' (actor="", tenant="", no detail) from the route. There is no audit record naming WHICH records (collection/ids/count per collection) were deleted or held. When a regulator asks 'what did you delete under retention and when', the tamper-evident audit chain cannot answer — deletion of consent proofs / DSARs / breach records happens without a witnessed, per-run detail entry.
findings.evidence:
await self._store.delete(collection, row["id"])
            purged += 1
findings.recommendation: Emit an audit record after the run with per-collection purged/held counts (and ideally the id ranges), so retention-driven deletions are as auditable as erasure and hold actions.

findings.title: Race between erase() and a concurrent proof append leaves raw subject behind and can collide the seq counter
findings.scenario: erase() pages proofs and pseudonymises them, then deletes the per-subject proof-seq row (line 127). If a consent proof is appended (ConsentStore.add_proof) for that subject AFTER the erase page loop has passed but before/around the seq delete, the new proof (a) keeps the RAW subject (never pseudonymised) and (b) the seq counter it allocated is then deleted, so the NEXT proof restarts at seq=1 and collides with an existing insertion-order id — forking the tamper-evident grant-before-withdraw ordering the store guarantees.
findings.evidence: await self._store.delete(_PROOF_SEQ, f"{tenant}::{subject}")
findings.recommendation: Serialise erase against consent writes for a subject (e.g. a per-subject lock/tombstone that makes post-erase grants refuse or re-pseudonymise), and re-scan proofs after deleting the seq row, or rebuild the seq from surviving proofs (as backup import does) rather than deleting it blind.

findings.title: Retention's legal-hold check cannot protect pseudonymised proof rows (hold keyed by raw subject)
findings.scenario: _is_held(row) calls holds.active_for(tenant, row['subject']). After erasure, a retained consent_proof row's subject is a pseudonym (sub_...), while legal holds are stored under the RAW subject. active_for(tenant, 'sub_...') matches nothing, so a consent proof that is under an active legal hold is treated as unheld and purged by retention once past its configured period — deleting evidence the hold was placed to preserve. A hold does NOT beat retention for pseudonymised rows, contradicting the module's stated invariant.
findings.recommendation: Intersect a pseudonymised row's subject_ref against held_refs (subject_ref of held subjects) as well as the raw active_for check, so a hold on the underlying person protects the pseudonymised evidence.

findings.title: Malformed security-policy JSON silently parses to {} (fail-open) instead of failing boot
findings.scenario: _json_any_map swallows malformed/typo'd JSON and returns {}. It backs INTERNAL_ROUTE_POLICY_JSON, INTERNAL_CALLER_PUBLIC_KEYS_JSON, INTERNAL_CALLER_JWKS_JSON and RATELIMIT_ROUTES. A misconfigured INTERNAL_ROUTE_POLICY_JSON (e.g. a trailing comma) becomes an EMPTY policy — and an absent route policy is default-open (any authenticated caller admitted), so a config typo silently widens the internal tier rather than refusing to start. Contrast the privacy_targets/retention_rules parsers, which correctly raise on malformed input.
findings.recommendation: For security-bearing maps, raise ValueError on malformed JSON (fail-fast) as privacy_targets does, rather than degrading to {} which is fail-open for a default-open policy layer.

findings.title: Cross-tenant open-DSAR / active-hold listings return raw subject and full payload for every tenant
findings.scenario: list_all_open returns d.public() for every tenant's open DSARs; public() drops only verification_token, so it still exposes the RAW subject id and the full request payload (which may hold correction/export PII) across all tenants. A single platform.compliance token thus yields a bulk cross-tenant harvest of raw subject identifiers. The read is audited and capability-gated, but it hands back raw PII where pseudonyms or a minimal projection would suffice for a triage list.
findings.evidence:
dsars, cursor = await self._dsars.open_dsars(limit=limit, after=after)
        out = []
        for d in dsars:
            item = d.public()
            item["overdue"] = d.overdue(now)
findings.recommendation: For the cross-tenant triage view, project a minimal shape (id, tenant, type, status, deadline, overdue) and pseudonymise the subject; omit payload. Fetch full detail only on a per-DSAR, per-tenant drill-down.

findings.title: Consent check cache can answer 'allowed' for up to the TTL after a guardian consent lapses at majority
findings.scenario: check() caches the full result (including allowed:true and notice_version) for CONSENT_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS. The generation counter is bumped only on grant/withdraw, never by the passage of time. A delegated (guardian) consent that lapses at the subject's majority instant (a time event) continues to be served as allowed:true from cache until the TTL expires — a window (default 30s, but configurable higher) of processing personal data on consent that is no longer lawful.
findings.recommendation: Do not cache a granted result for a delegated consent whose majority_at is within the TTL window (or cache with an expiry clamped to majority_at), so a lapse takes effect at the instant it occurs rather than up to a TTL later.

findings.title: release_hold lacks the cross-tenant `tenant` param that verify/process have; its audit scope diverges from the release scope
findings.scenario: verify_dsar and process_dsar accept a `tenant` query so a platform.compliance officer can act on a hold/DSAR they discovered cross-tenant. release_hold does not: it scopes with _tenant(principal) (no body/query), so a platform officer with tenant=None resolves to 'global' and cannot release a hold discovered in any real shop — the very holds surfaced by the cross-tenant list_open_holds view are unreleasable. Separately, the write-ahead audit uses tenant=principal.tenant while the release uses _tenant(principal), so the recorded tenant can differ from the tenant actually acted on.
findings.evidence:
await request.app.state.auditor.record(
        "legal_hold.released", actor=principal.subject, tenant=principal.tenant, resource=f"hold:{hold_id}", ...)
    h = await build_compliance(request).release_hold(hold_id, tenant=_tenant(principal))
findings.recommendation: Add a `tenant` query param honoured for platform.compliance (as verify/process do), and record the audit tenant using the same _tenant(principal, tenant) value used for the release.

findings.title: ERASURE and CORRECTION DSARs are processed with NO identity verification
findings.scenario: process() gates verification only for ACCESS and EXPORT. An ERASURE (destructive) or CORRECTION DSAR reaches the target fan-out with d.verified=False. Any caller who can create+process a DSAR (compliance.manage, held by tenant admins) can trigger irreversible erasure of a named subject's data across every registered target without any proof the request came from the subject — a data-destruction / denial vector, and a way to weaponise erasure against a specific person. The 'identity before PII' guard protects reads but not the more damaging writes.
findings.evidence:
if d.type in (ACCESS, EXPORT) and not d.verified:
            return {"ok": False, "reason": "NOT_VERIFIED"}
findings.recommendation: Require verification (or an explicit, audited operator override with a documented lawful basis) before processing ERASURE/CORRECTION too, or clearly document and separately gate the operator-initiated destructive path with a stronger capability than compliance.manage.

findings.title: target-ack audit always records tenant="" because ack_target never returns a tenant
findings.scenario: target_ack records the DSAR-completing 'dsar.target_acked' event with tenant=res.get("tenant", ""). DsarService.ack_target returns {"ok", "status", "remaining"} — there is no 'tenant' key — so every target-ack audit entry is written with an empty tenant. The entry that closes a DSAR (an assertion that personal data was destroyed) is un-attributable to a tenant in the audit trail.
findings.evidence:
await request.app.state.auditor.record(
        "dsar.target_acked", actor=f"service:{body.service}", tenant=res.get("tenant", ""), ...)
findings.recommendation: Have ack_target return the DSAR's tenant (it has d.tenant in hand) and record it, or look up the DSAR's tenant in the route before recording.

findings.title: _tenant() 'global' fallback silently targets a real tenant named 'global' on write paths
findings.scenario: For a platform.compliance principal with no body tenant and no principal.tenant, _tenant returns the literal 'global'. On write routes (grant, withdraw with no body.tenant) this silently writes consent/proof rows under a tenant literally named 'global' — colliding with any real shop provisioned as 'global' and mixing platform-op writes into it. The same string-literal fallback previously caused the documented cross-tenant list bug.
findings.recommendation: Require an explicit tenant for platform-op WRITE routes (reject when none is supplied) rather than defaulting to a guessable literal that can be a real tenant name.

findings.title: verify_dsar returns HTTP 400 for NOT_FOUND instead of 404
findings.scenario: verify() returns reason NOT_FOUND when the DSAR does not exist or is owned by another tenant, but the route maps every non-ok result to HTTP 400. A missing/other-tenant DSAR should be 404 (as process_dsar and the ack routes correctly return); returning 400 conflates a bad-request with a not-found and diverges from the contract the other DSAR routes follow.
findings.recommendation: Map NOT_FOUND → 404, TOKEN_EXPIRED/BAD_TOKEN → 400/401, consistent with process_dsar and target_ack.

findings.title: is_subject_ref uses a length-only check, so a crafted raw subject can dodge pseudonymisation/erasure
findings.scenario: is_subject_ref returns True for any string that starts with 'sub_' and is 36 chars — it does NOT verify the tail is hex. A raw subject identifier of the form 'sub_' + 32 arbitrary chars is treated as an already-wrapped pseudonym: subject_ref() returns it unchanged (never hashed), so it is written verbatim into 'immutable' records, and erase-time double-wrap protection misfires. An attacker choosing such a subject id embeds a raw value where a pseudonym is expected.
findings.evidence: return isinstance(value, str) and value.startswith(_PREFIX) and len(value) == len(_PREFIX) + _LEN
findings.recommendation: Also require the 32-char tail to be lowercase hex (e.g. regex ^sub_[0-9a-f]{32}$) before treating a value as an existing pseudonym.

findings.title: Per-tenant GET /dsar ignores pagination (`after`), capping a tenant to its newest 100 DSARs
findings.scenario: The non-platform branch of list_dsar calls build_dsar().list(tenant), which reads COMPLIANCE_LIST_LIMIT (100) newest DSARs with no cursor passthrough — the route's `after`/`limit` query params are honoured only on the platform cross-tenant branch. A tenant with more than 100 DSARs cannot page to older requests through its own listing endpoint.
findings.evidence: return {"requests": await build_dsar(request).list(_tenant(principal, tenant))}
findings.recommendation: Thread limit/after into DsarService.list (DsarStore.list already accepts after) and return next_cursor for the per-tenant branch too.

findings.title: Guardian consent audit is recorded fail-open AFTER the write, though it is the disputable claim
findings.scenario: The grant route records 'consent.guardian_recorded' AFTER the store write and treats the whole grant path as fail-open (auditor never refuses). But the route's own comment calls delegated consent 'the claim someone may later dispute' — exactly the class of action the write-ahead/fail-closed pattern (used for withdraw, process, holds) exists for. If the audit sink is unavailable when a guardian consent is granted, the consent is persisted with no witness of who recorded it, on what basis, for whom.
findings.recommendation: Treat guardian/legal_representative consent as a critical, write-ahead (fail-closed) audit action so a delegated-capacity claim cannot be recorded unwitnessed, while keeping self-consent fail-open.

findings.title: Internal read twins exposing PII are default-open with token fallback enabled
findings.scenario: internal_consent_history, internal_dsar and consent-check return a named subject's consent/DSAR history (raw PII) for an arbitrary tenant/subject. They are guarded only by require_internal_token; INTERNAL_ROUTE_POLICY_JSON is empty by default (any authenticated caller admitted) and INTERNAL_CALLER_ALLOW_TOKEN_FALLBACK defaults True. So any holder of the shared internal token can enumerate consent/DSAR PII for any tenant/subject, with no per-route caller allowlist. It is the documented trust boundary, but these particular PII-returning reads have no tighter default than the hot-path checks.
findings.evidence:
@router.get("/compliance/consent-history", dependencies=[Depends(require_internal_token)])
async def internal_consent_history(... tenant ..., subject ...):
findings.recommendation: Ship a default INTERNAL_ROUTE_POLICY_JSON entry restricting the PII-returning read twins to the specific investigation/report-generator caller identities, and plan to disable the token fallback once callers sign assertions.
